Riding the TT Course: A Pilgrimage for Every Motorcyclist

The Isle of Man TT Mountain Course is the most famous motorcycle road circuit in the world. At 37.73 miles per lap, it uses public roads that are open to all traffic outside race periods. Riding the course at road-legal speeds is a bucket-list experience for any motorcyclist — and it's far more accessible than you might think.

The Course Overview

The TT course starts and finishes on Glencrutchery Road in Douglas and runs anticlockwise around the island. It passes through villages, over open mountain, and along some of the most varied road scenery in Britain. The course record stands at an average speed of over 135mph — at road speeds, expect the lap to take about 90 minutes with a few stops.

Key Sections

The Start to Ballacraine: Through the suburbs of Douglas and out into the countryside. Bray Hill, the famous plunging start, drops steeply and bears left — even at 30mph it gives a taste of what the racers face at 170mph.

Ballacraine to Ramsey: The longest section, passing through Kirk Michael, Ballaugh (famous for its bridge jump), and Sulby. The Sulby Straight is the fastest part of the course — racers exceed 200mph here. At road speeds, it's a long, straight blast through farmland.

The Mountain Section

From Ramsey, the course climbs the Mountain Road — the most spectacular section. The road rises to 422 metres with views across the entire island and, on clear days, to Scotland, England, Ireland, and Wales simultaneously. The mountain section is exposed to weather and can be foggy even when the coast is clear.

Riding the TT course at road speed is humbling. You realise just how narrow, bumpy, and unforgiving these roads are — and how extraordinary the racers are to lap them at race speed.

Corner-by-Corner Highlights

  • Bray Hill — The iconic plunging start, take it steady
  • Union Mills — Tight village section with houses lining the road
  • Ballaugh Bridge — The famous humpback where bikes go airborne in the race
  • Gooseneck — Tight hairpin on the Mountain climb
  • The Verandah — Exposed mountain section with sheer drops
  • Creg-ny-Baa — Famous viewing point with a pub, perfect for a mid-lap drink
  • Governor's Bridge — The final bend before the finish line

When to Visit

The course is open to ride year-round except during race closures. TT fortnight (late May/early June) and the Manx Grand Prix (August) see the course closed for practice and racing. Visit outside these periods for a quieter experience, or during race weeks for the atmosphere. The island has a national speed limit of unrestricted on some derestricted roads, but ride responsibly — the course is a public road with junctions, pedestrians, and oncoming traffic.

Getting There

The Isle of Man Steam Packet operates ferries from Heysham, Liverpool, and Dublin. Book motorcycle spaces early, especially during race periods. The crossing takes 2.5-4 hours depending on the port. The island has fuel stations in every town and plentiful accommodation.

faq.q: Can I ride the TT course myself?
faq.a: Yes. The 37.73-mile Mountain Course uses public roads that are open to all traffic outside race periods, so riding it at road-legal speeds is a genuine bucket-list experience. Expect a lap to take about 90 minutes with a few stops, and treat it as the public road it is.

The course is open to ride year-round except during race closures. TT fortnight in late May and early June, and the Manx Grand Prix in August, see the course closed for practice and racing. Visit outside these periods for a quieter experience, or during race weeks for the atmosphere.

faq.q: How do I get to the Isle of Man with a motorcycle?
faq.a: The Isle of Man Steam Packet operates ferries from Heysham, Liverpool and Dublin, with crossings of 2.5 to 4 hours depending on the port. Book motorcycle spaces early, especially during race periods, as they sell out fast. The island has fuel stations in every town and plentiful accommodation.

faq.q: Is it safe to ride the course at speed?
faq.a: Ride responsibly. Although some derestricted mountain sections have no speed limit, the course is a public road with junctions, pedestrians and oncoming traffic. Riding it at road speed is humbling, revealing just how narrow, bumpy and unforgiving these roads are compared with what the racers achieve.
